<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>N6-methyladenosine (m6A) represents a prevalent internal epitranscriptomic modification of mRNA that influences post-transcriptional gene regulation. Clinically, ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury contributes to tissue damage in acute kidney injury, ischemic stroke, and myocardial infarction, particularly after blood flow is restored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We searched Google Scholar, Web of Science, and PubMed for literature published through May 2026. The retrieval focused on articles detailing how m6A effector proteins—specifically writers, erasers, and readers—mediate I/R pathogenesis within hepatic, renal, cardiac, and cerebral tissues.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>m6A-associated regulation influences RNA metabolism during I/R injury. Context-dependent changes in m6A regulators and target transcripts are linked to oxidative stress, inflammatory cascades, and specific programmed cell death pathways, including ferroptosis and pyroptosis, across various organ systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Profiling these organ-specific m6A molecular networks may inform future research on targeted epitranscriptomic interventions for IRI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Regulatory roles and molecular mechanisms of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification in ischemia-reperfusion injury

<jats:p>
                    This study aimed to isolate and characterize individual hepatitis B virus (HBV) strains from a patient co-infected with genotype B and C, and to directly compare their intrinsic replication capacities. HBV DNA was isolated from a chronic hepatitis B patient. Genotypes were determined by genotype-specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and full-length genomes were cloned. Two clones representing subgenotype B2 (c17) and C1 (c21) were selected, sequenced and transfected into HepG2 cells. Viral replication was assessed
                    <jats:italic>via</jats:italic>
                    Southern blot and quantitative PCR. The role of the common Adenine (A)1762Thymine (T/)Guanine (G)1764A mutation in the C1 clone was investigated by site-directed mutagenesis. As a result, the genotype C1 clone exhibited significantly higher replication capacity than the B2 clone. Counterintuitively, reverting the A1762T/G1764A mutation in the C1 clone to wild-type further enhanced its replication, indicating this mutation was not the primary driver of its high replicative fitness. In conclusion, HBV genotype C1 possesses a greater inherent replication capacity than B2, independent of the classic basal core promoter (BCP) mutation, providing a virological explanation for its association with severe disease outcomes in co-infection.
                  </jats:p>
title: Intrinsic replication advantage of a Hepatitis B Virus genotype C strain is independent of the basal core promoter A1762T/G1764A mutation

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Public awareness of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is limited worldwide, with potential implications for timely recognition, care seeking, and social support. Data from the Northern Border Region of Saudi Arabia are lacking. This study aims to assess community awareness and knowledge of ALS and identify predictors of good awareness among adults in the Northern Border Region of Saudi Arabia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional survey of 1,277 adults used a structured self-administered questionnaire covering sociodemographic characteristics, general awareness, knowledge, attitudes, personal experience, and information sources. Awareness was scored from 16 knowledge items and categorized as good (≥ 60%) or poor (<60%). Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests with Cramér’s V, and multivariable logistic regression were applied; model performance was assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test and area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants were mainly young to middle-aged, female, and university-educated, and most worked outside the health field. Although 45.2% had heard of ALS, 90.8% showed poor awareness, while only 9.2% showed good awareness. Uncertainty predominated regarding prognosis, risk groups, neuroanatomical involvement, non-motor symptoms, curability, and diagnostic difficulty. Age and occupation were associated with awareness in bivariate analyses but lost significance after adjustment. Never having heard of ALS markedly reduced the odds of good awareness (adjusted odds ratio (AOR) = 0.167, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.097–0.288],
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      < 0.001), while using the internet and healthcare sources was associated with higher awareness. The model showed good calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.891) and discrimination (AUC = 0.820).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Community awareness and knowledge of ALS in this region are poor, underscoring the need for targeted digital and healthcare-based educational initiatives to improve ALS literacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Community awareness and knowledge of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a cross-sectional study in the Northern Border Region of Saudi Arabia

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High-throughput bisulfite sequencing (BS-seq), including whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) and reduced representation bisulfite sequencing (RRBS), provides base-resolution DNA methylation. Despite mature command-line (CLI) workflows for alignment, methylation calling and downstream analysis, many researchers without CLI experience face steep setup and reproducibility barriers. Existing graphic user interfaces (GUIs) often target array data or late-stage visualization and rarely assist with containerized, sequencing-oriented workflows that must run on high-performance computing (HPC) cluster or local workstations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We present
                      <jats:italic>methylEZ</jats:italic>
                      , an open-source, cross-platform, Python/Tkinter GUI that streamlines preparation of BS-seq analyses while preserving transparent, script-first execution. The application is organized in three modules: (1) preprocessing: FAST-All with Quality (FASTQ) selection, read-pairing, and generation of validated samplesheets and ready-to-run commands for the nf-core/methylseq pipeline; (2) quality control assistance:automation of common asset preparation (reference indexing/dictionaries, Browser Extensible Data (BED) to Picard interval_list conversion, Binary Alignment Map (BAM) sorting/indexing) and batch scripts to drive Picard tools (
                      <jats:italic>e.g</jats:italic>
                      ., CollectHsMetrics for capture designs) and samtools; and (3) downstream analysis templating: export of a parameterizable methylKit R script supporting coverage filters, differential methylation (DM) detection (with optional tiling), basic plots and annotation. All artifacts (CLI strings, configs and scripts) are saved for inspection, version control and reuse.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We validated
                      <jats:italic>methylEZ</jats:italic>
                      on in-house methyl-capture BS-seq data and on publicly available BS-seq data. The GUI correctly produced nf-core/methylseq samplesheets and Nextflow commands, and the quality control (QC) module batched reference/BAM preparations and coverage summaries
                      <jats:italic>via</jats:italic>
                      scripted Picard/samtools steps, reducing repetitive CLI interaction. The exported methylKit templates executed without error and generated interpretable differential methylation outputs.
                      <jats:italic>methylEZ</jats:italic>
                      runs on macOS, Windows and Linux; it is installable
                      <jats:italic>via</jats:italic>
                      pip from GitHub and requires Python 3; Tkinter is bundled on Windows/macOS and typically available
                      <jats:italic>via</jats:italic>
                      the Tk package on Linux.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:italic>methylEZ</jats:italic>
                      lowers the entry barrier to reproducible BS-seq by moving error-prone configuration and QC setup into a guided GUI while keeping execution explicit and auditable through exported commands and scripts. The tool complements web platforms (
                      <jats:italic>e.g</jats:italic>
                      ., Galaxy) by emphasizing offline control and compatibility with community workflows (nf-core/methylseq) and statistical packages (methylKit) on capable infrastructure. Planned extensions include in-GUI visualization (
                      <jats:italic>e.g</jats:italic>
                      ., PCA, coverage histograms, volcano plots) and support for alternative callers and statistical frameworks.
                      <jats:italic>methylEZ</jats:italic>
                      is released under GPL-3.0.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aims</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Seedling and sapling community assembly is a key process affecting forest regeneration and succession, yet the spatial aggregation patterns and assembly mechanisms of locally regenerating communities in broad-leaved Korean pine (
                      <jats:italic>Pinus koraiensis</jats:italic>
                      ) forests remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we identified aggregation scales and patch sizes and elucidated the assembly mechanisms of local seedling and sapling communities.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted stand and regeneration surveys in four broad-leaved Korean pine forest plots. For each regenerating individual, we recorded its species identity, spatial position, and height. Leaf traits were measured at the species level, and local canopy environmental variables were quantified based on stand survey data. Ripley’s
                      <jats:italic>g(r)</jats:italic>
                      , fitted using a Thomas process with a two-nested-scale function, was used to identify aggregation scales, and hierarchical clustering was used to delineate local communities. Abundance-based and presence-based standardized effect sizes of mean pairwise trait distance (SES.MPD), standardized effect sizes of Pielou’s evenness (SES.E), and the degree of distribution tendency (
                      <jats:italic>D</jats:italic>
                      ) were then used to characterize community structure, and redundancy analysis (RDA) was used to assess trait–environment relationships.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Both local seedling and sapling communities exhibited two characteristic aggregation scales, at approximately 1 and 15 m. Compared with sapling communities, seedling communities showed stronger aggregation at both the small and large scales, had more patches and more individuals per patch. Across 1–15 m scales, abundance-weighted
                      <jats:italic>SES.MPD</jats:italic>
                      , presence-based
                      <jats:italic>SES.MPD</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>SES.E</jats:italic>
                      , and their corresponding
                      <jats:italic>D</jats:italic>
                      values indicated non-random functional structure in both communities, with stronger abundance-based patterns in seedlings but more consistent presence-based patterns in saplings, and stronger signals of competition at smaller scales in saplings. The RDA showed that environmental explanatory power was relatively weak overall, but increased with spatial scale and developmental stage. Compared with the seedling communities, the sapling communities demonstrated weaker or even opposite correlations in community-weighted mean leaf area (CWM.LA), specific leaf area (SLA), and leaf width (LW) with vertical distribution tendency degrees and local coniferous leaf area index.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, stochastic processes played a major role in shaping local regeneration communities. Limited dispersal caused regenerating individuals with similar traits to cluster across spatial scales. As seedlings developed into saplings, the influence of canopy conditions progressively accumulated, and local competition apparently became stronger, especially at small spatial scales. These findings suggest that the mechanisms shaping regeneration communities change during development, and that seedlings and saplings respond differently to canopy structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Marine bacteria are important sources of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes, but the amylolytic activity of many non-model marine bacterial lineages remains insufficiently characterized at the phenotype level. This study evaluated extracellular amylolytic activity in the marine isolate
                      <jats:italic>Croceibacter</jats:italic>
                      sp. 23-6 and examined its metal-ion response and wheat starch hydrolysis performance under defined laboratory conditions.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Strain 23-6 was isolated from mesopelagic seawater of the western Pacific Ocean and identified at the genus level using 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis. Extracellular amylolytic activity was first screened on starch agar. A partially purified extracellular amylolytic protein preparation was then used to determine the effects of temperature, pH, thermal and pH stability, metal ions, apparent kinetic parameters and hydrolysis of different starch substrates. Wheat starch hydrolysis was further evaluated using single-factor experiments and response surface methodology based on a Box–Behnken design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Strain 23-6 produced a clear starch-hydrolysis halo and was conservatively assigned to the genus
                      <jats:italic>Croceibacter</jats:italic>
                      . The partially purified extracellular protein fraction showed maximum amylolytic activity at 50 °C and pH 7.0 and retained comparatively higher activity under near-neutral conditions. Among the tested metal ions, Cu
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      increased the measured relative activity to 119.0% at 3 mM, whereas K
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      , Mn
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      , Zn
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      and Fe
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      decreased the measured activity. Wheat starch showed the highest relative reducing-sugar release among the tested insoluble starch substrates. Response surface optimization predicted suitable hydrolysis conditions of approximately 52 min, 50 °C, 4.0 U/mL enzyme and 1.0% wheat starch. Validation under the adjusted conditions yielded 2.43 ± 0.09 mg/mL reducing sugars, expressed as maltose equivalents, consistent with the model prediction.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      These results provide strain-level evidence that
                      <jats:italic>Croceibacter</jats:italic>
                      sp. 23-6 exhibits extracellular amylolytic activity and indicate that its partially purified extracellular protein fraction displays a measurable Cu
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      -responsive activity profile and wheat starch hydrolysis capacity. The findings define the functional properties of this marine bacterial extracellular amylolytic fraction while leaving the identity of the responsible enzyme(s), preparation homogeneity, and the mechanism of Cu
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      response for future work.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To investigate the relationship between iron metabolism and all-cause mortality in patients with sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The clinical data of SA-AKI patients from the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University were analyzed retrospectively. All patients were followed up for 90 days, after which they were divided into survival and death groups Cox regression analysis was used to explore the risk factors for all-cause death in patients with SA-AKI. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and Kaplan–Meier curves were used to analyze the relationship between different iron metabolism indexes and prognosis in patients with SA-AKI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 3,049 SA-AKI patients were included, with a male-to-female ratio of 1.22:1 and an average age of 64.32 ± 16.46 years. Of these patients, 40.0% underwent renal replacement therapy (RRT), 21.4% received invasive mechanical ventilation, 14.5% received transfusions, and 44.8% were treated with vasoactive drugs. The 90-day all-cause mortality was 20.5%. The area under the curve (AUC) for the combined indexes of iron metabolism (serum iron, serum ferritin (SF) , and transferrin (TRF)) for predicting all-cause mortality in SA-AKI patients was 0.757. Kaplan–Meier survival curves revealed that the 90-day cumulative survival rate of the increased serum iron, increased SF and decreased TRF groups were significantly lower than that of the normal group. Multivariate Cox regression analysis revealed that the increased serum iron concentration, and SF concentration; decreased TRF concentration were independent risk factors for 90-day all-cause death in SA-AKI patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Elevated serum iron and SF concentrations and decreased TRF concentration are important factors affecting the mortality of patients with SA-AKI. Abnormal iron metabolism indexes in patients with SA-AKI may be associated with a high risk of all-cause death.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Influence of iron metabolism on all-cause death in patients with sepsis-associated acute kidney injury: a retrospective cohort study

<jats:p>
                    Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by behavioral traits such as inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, has been widely associated with mental health impairments. However, the presence of these traits alone does not determine diagnosis, as they must also cause significant functional impairment for the individual to fulfill diagnostic criteria. Therefore, this study aimed at exploring how ADHD traits are associated with mental health indicators in general population adults regardless of whether participants met full diagnostic criteria for the disorder. The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) was used to screen ADHD traits in an online survey that also addressed mental health indicators such as excessive preoccupation, lack of meaning in life and substance use. Invitations were distributed
                    <jats:italic>via</jats:italic>
                    social media platforms. The final sample consisted of 2,159 Brazilian adult participants. Data were analyzed using network analysis. An undirected network was modeled using the Gaussian Graphical Model based on partial polychoric correlations, and regularization was applied using EBICglasso. The main network analysis was conducted for individual ADHD traits. Additional analyses were performed for the summed inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity scores, for the total ASRS summed score, and for subgroups of participants exhibiting extreme levels of trait presentation. Results indicate that, in an adult community sample, association between ADHD traits and mental health impairment is predominantly indirect. This indirect association was commonly interposed by younger age and feelings of insecurity. The results were consistent across all analyses. Overall, our results suggest that the presence of ADHD traits alone is not strongly associated with mental health impairment in the general population. We propose that both research and clinical practice may benefit from further exploring and addressing intervening factors—such as insecurity—that could underlie the association between ADHD traits and mental health impairment observed in previous studies.
                  </jats:p>
title: Network analysis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder traits and mental health indicators in Brazilian adults

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overweight and obesity are common among middle-aged and older adults, and obesity is a chronic, multifactorial disease that, particularly when accompanied by central adiposity or metabolic abnormalities, is associated with increased cardiometabolic, cancer-related, musculoskeletal, and functional risks. Leptin and ghrelin are key hormones involved in energy balance regulation and may be dysregulated in obesity, but evidence regarding the effects of exercise interventions on leptin and ghrelin levels in middle-aged and older adults with overweight or obesity remains inconsistent. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of exercise interventions on leptin and ghrelin levels in this population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and CNKI were searched from database inception to 5 July 2026. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials that enrolled middle-aged or older adults with overweight or obesity and reported leptin or ghrelin levels before and after an exercise intervention. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were synthesized using Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 15. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using
                      <jats:italic>I</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      ; a fixed-effect model was used when
                      <jats:italic>I</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      < 50%, and a random-effects model when
                      <jats:italic>I</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      ≥ 50%. Subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, and publication-bias assessments were conducted.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Twenty-one randomized controlled trials were included. Exercise interventions were associated with significantly lower leptin levels than control conditions based on 18 comparisons (SMD = −0.32, 95% CI [−0.47 to −0.18],
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      < 0.0001), with low between-study heterogeneity (
                      <jats:italic>
                        I
                        <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      </jats:italic>
                      = 22%). Exercise interventions were also associated with significantly higher ghrelin levels based on nine comparisons (SMD = 0.45, 95% CI [0.11–0.79],
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.01), although heterogeneity was substantial (
                      <jats:italic>I</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 74%). Subgroup analyses suggested that exercise-related characteristics may partly contribute to variability in leptin and ghrelin responses, but these findings were exploratory. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses supported the stability of the main estimates. For leptin, Egger’s test suggested possible funnel-plot asymmetry, but trim-and-fill analysis did not impute any missing comparison and the pooled estimate remained unchanged.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Exercise interventions were associated with reduced leptin levels and increased ghrelin levels in middle-aged and older adults with overweight or obesity. The leptin finding appeared relatively consistent, whereas the ghrelin finding should be interpreted cautiously because of fewer comparisons and substantial heterogeneity. Subgroup findings remain exploratory and should not be used to define an optimal exercise prescription. Further randomized controlled trials with more standardized exercise protocols, clearer dietary control, and consistent hormone measurement are needed to clarify the clinical relevance of these changes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Effects of exercise interventions on leptin and ghrelin levels in middle-aged and older adults with overweight or obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT) is a key driver of atherosclerosis (AS). This study integrated multiple RNA transcriptomic and single-cell transcriptomic datasets to identify shared gene expression signatures between EndMT and AS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      GEO expression profiles were analyzed
                      <jats:italic>via</jats:italic>
                      differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and functional enrichment analyses. A Random Forest model evaluated key genes, validating their expression and diagnostic performance. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) further assessed their expression patterns, and a Transcription Factor (TF)-mRNA-miRNA regulatory network.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Fifteen overlapping genes were identified, from which six candidates were screened through a Protein-Protein Interaction (PPI) network and validated
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      . The application of a Random Forest model identified two key hub genes,
                      <jats:italic>CCL5</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic>IL1B</jats:italic>
                      , which were significantly upregulated. Their diagnostic Area Under the Curve (AUC) was >0.7 when assessed separately and increased to >0.85 in a combined model. Three shared TFs (NFKBIA, NFKB1, RELA) of the Nuclear Factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway were identified, highlighting its central role in disease progression.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:italic>CCL5</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic>IL1B</jats:italic>
                      are key genes potentially regulating EndMT-mediated AS
                      <jats:italic>via</jats:italic>
                      inflammatory pathways including Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like (NOD-like) receptor, Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF), and NF-κB signaling, offering promising diagnostic and therapeutic targets for AS.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Identifying potential targets in endothelial to mesenchymal transition-mediated atherosclerosis using bioinformatics and machine learning

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Effective blocking is an important contributor to match outcomes in volleyball. However, the phase-specific kinematic characteristics associated with approach velocity (AV) and jump height (JH) during cross-step blocking have not been comprehensively examined. This study aimed to identify the kinematic variables associated with AV and JH during right-side cross-step blocking in elite youth male volleyball players.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This cross-sectional study included 22 elite youth male volleyball players performing right-side cross-step blocking under standardized conditions, with each participant’s highest-rated eligible trial selected for kinematic analysis based on assessments by two volleyball experts. Kinematic data were recorded using two high-speed video cameras and processed with Fastmove Motion-3D software. Correlation analyses were conducted to identify kinematic variables associated with AV and JH, with
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      values adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Variables that remained significant after FDR correction were subsequently examined using univariable linear regression, followed by parsimonious multivariable linear regression where appropriate.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      For AV, five kinematic variables remained significantly associated with AV after FDR correction: third-step right hip linear velocity (R-LVH-TS,
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.80, FDR
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), second-step left knee angular velocity (L-AVK-SS,
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.71, FDR
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                       = 0.003), second-step left hip linear velocity (L-LVH-SS,
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.62, FDR
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                       = 0.015), second-step foot displacement (SFD,
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.61, FDR
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                       = 0.015), and third-step right knee linear velocity (R-LVK-TS,
                      <jats:italic>ρ</jats:italic>
                       = 0.67, FDR
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                       = 0.007). In univariable linear regression models, these variables explained 63.5%, 50.7%, 38.8%, 37.8%, and 24.7% of the variance in AV, respectively. The parsimonious multivariable regression model including third-step right hip linear velocity and second-step left knee angular velocity explained 67.7% of the variance in AV. In this model, only third-step right hip linear velocity remained independently associated with AV. For JH, take-off-phase center-of-mass (CoM) linear velocity was the only variable that remained significantly associated with JH after FDR correction (LVCoM-TO,
                      <jats:italic>ρ</jats:italic>
                       = 0.65, FDR
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                       = 0.025), explaining 57.9% of the variance in JH in the univariable regression model.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that AV during right-side cross-step blocking is related to phase-specific lower-limb kinematic coordination during second- and third-step phases, especially right hip linear velocity during the third step. JH is associated with greater CoM linear velocity during take-off. In practice, third-step right hip linear velocity and take-off-phase CoM linear velocity may serve as biomechanical reference points for evaluating approach and jump performance, respectively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Kinematic characteristics associated with right-side cross-step blocking performance in elite youth male volleyball players: a cross-sectional study

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Gastric cancer (GC) remains among the most common and lethal malignancies worldwide. The identification of novel biomarkers is critical for improving prognostic evaluation and informing therapeutic decision-making. Methyltransferase-like 6 (METTL6), a transfer RNA methyltransferase implicated in cell division, has a poorly defined biological role and mechanism in GC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      METTL6 expression was systematically investigated using experimental techniques and bioinformatic analyses. Comprehensive clinical and pathological data were collected to stratify patients with GC for comparative evaluation. Kaplan–Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression models were applied to determine the prognostic significance of METTL6 expression. In parallel, immune cell infiltration associated with METTL6 expression was analyzed using data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, and the prognostic impact of METTL6 was further assessed within immune infiltration–defined subgroups. METTL6 knockdown was achieved through lentiviral transduction, and its biological effects were examined both
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic>in vivo</jats:italic>
                      using colony formation, wound healing, Transwell migration and invasion assays, and xenograft mouse models.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      METTL6 was markedly overexpressed in GC cell lines. Elevated METTL6 expression was significantly associated with sex, clinical stage, histological type, histological grade, and poorer overall survival. In addition, METTL6 expression demonstrated a strong correlation with immune cell infiltration. Functional experiments showed that METTL6 knockdown significantly inhibited colony formation, wound closure, and tumor cell migration and invasion
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      . Consistently, METTL6 silencing substantially reduced tumor volume and tumor weight in xenograft-bearing mice.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>METTL6 overexpression is closely associated with an unfavorable prognosis in GC and may represent a valuable prognostic biomarker. Furthermore, METTL6 warrants further investigation as a potential therapeutic target.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Role of METTL6 in gastric cancer: diagnostic, prognostic, and functional implications
